questions.stem: In *perfect competition*, the demand curve faced by an individual firm is *most likely*:

choices.text: Downward-sloping.
Perfectly elastic (horizontal).
Upward-sloping.

questions.explanation:
Perfect competition: many firms, homogeneous products, no individual firm has market power. Each firm is a price taker — its individual demand curve is perfectly elastic at the market price.

**A** describes monopolistic competition or monopoly.
**C** is economically rare for demand curves.

questions.stem: In long-run equilibrium under perfect competition, firms *most likely* earn:

choices.text: Positive economic profit.
Zero economic profit.
Negative economic profit.

questions.explanation:
Free entry/exit drives economic profit to zero in long-run equilibrium. New entrants compete away positive profits; firms exit if losses sustained.

**A** would attract entrants until profits compete away.
**C** would prompt exits until profits return to zero.

questions.stem: The *kinked demand model* of oligopoly *most likely* implies that:

choices.text: Prices in oligopolistic industries tend to be rigid.
Oligopoly prices change frequently with cost changes.
Oligopolists always engage in cutthroat price competition.

questions.explanation:
Kinked demand model: competitors match price decreases (to maintain share) but not increases (to gain share). Result: price increases lose share, price decreases trigger industry-wide drops — both punished, so prices tend to be rigid.

**B** is empirically observed less than the rigid pattern in many oligopolies.
**C** is rarely sustained — collusion or rigidity is more common.

questions.stem: A profit-maximising firm produces at the level where:

choices.text: Total revenue equals total cost.
Marginal revenue equals marginal cost.
Average cost is at its minimum.

questions.explanation:
MR = MC is the universal profit-maximisation rule, regardless of market structure. The price set depends on the demand curve faced (which varies by structure).

**A** is the breakeven point (zero profit).
**C** is one efficiency point but not the profit-max.

questions.stem: A monopoly *most likely* differs from perfect competition because:

choices.text: Monopoly produces less and sets a higher price than perfect competition.
Monopoly faces an elastic demand curve.
Monopoly's demand curve is unrelated to its pricing decision.

questions.explanation:
Monopoly restricts output (sets MR = MC where MR < demand) to maintain higher prices. Perfect competition produces more at lower prices because each firm is a price taker.

**B** is backwards — monopoly faces downward-sloping demand.
**C** is incorrect — the demand curve determines the price.

questions.stem: Sustained economic profits in any market structure *most likely* require:

choices.text: Durable barriers to entry that prevent competition from eroding profits.
Significant government subsidies.
Identical products to competitors.

questions.explanation:
Barriers to entry (scale, network effects, brand, switching costs, regulatory, IP) prevent competitors from competing away profits. Without barriers, free entry drives profits to zero in the long run.

**B** is occasionally a factor but not the general principle.
**C** would be perfect competition with zero economic profit.

questions.stem: The *four phases* of a typical business cycle are *most likely*:

choices.text: Expansion, peak, contraction, trough.
Birth, growth, maturity, decline.
Boom, bust, recovery, plateau.

questions.explanation:
Standard business cycle: expansion (growing), peak (highest point), contraction/recession (declining), trough (lowest point), then back to expansion.

**B** describes product life cycles.
**C** is informal language.

questions.stem: A *leading economic indicator* is one that *most likely*:

choices.text: Rises after the economy turns.
Rises before the broader economy turns.
Rises in lockstep with the broader economy.

questions.explanation:
Leading indicators precede economic turning points. Examples: stock market, building permits, durable goods orders, yield curve, consumer sentiment.

**A** describes lagging indicators.
**C** describes coincident indicators.

questions.stem: An inverted yield curve (short rates > long rates) *most likely* signals:

choices.text: Imminent economic expansion.
Increased recession probability (with variable lag).
Stable economic conditions.

questions.explanation:
Yield curve inversions have preceded most US recessions since 1960. Lag varies (months to 2+ years). Inversion 2022-2023 has been widely watched but timing variable.

**A** is reverse direction.
**C** misreads the signal.

questions.stem: Which sector is *most likely* defensive (less cyclically sensitive)?

choices.text: Auto manufacturers.
Consumer staples / supermarkets.
Construction.

questions.explanation:
Defensive sectors have demand relatively insensitive to economic cycles. People still need food, healthcare, basic necessities in recessions. Examples: staples, healthcare, utilities, telecoms.

**A** and **C** are cyclical — autos and construction track economy strongly.

questions.stem: Credit cycles *most likely* affect business cycles by:

choices.text: Amplifying both upturns (more lending) and downturns (lending pullback).
Working independently of business cycles.
Smoothing business cycle peaks and troughs.

questions.explanation:
Credit cycles tend to amplify business cycles: expansion drives lending which supports growth; contraction reduces lending which deepens recession. 2008 GFC is the classic example.

**B** is incorrect — they're tightly linked.
**C** is the opposite of what occurs.

questions.stem: Capacity utilisation above 80% *most likely* signals:

choices.text: Early-cycle, with slack and room for growth.
Late-cycle, with inflation and wage pressure building.
Recession territory.

questions.explanation:
High capacity utilisation = economy near full capacity. Inflation and wage pressures accumulate. Late-cycle indicator.

**A** is low capacity utilisation (under 70%).
**C** would also be low utilisation.

questions.stem: *Expansionary* fiscal policy *most likely* involves:

choices.text: Raising taxes and cutting spending.
Cutting taxes and increasing spending.
Holding policy unchanged.

questions.explanation:
Expansionary fiscal policy boosts aggregate demand: tax cuts (raise disposable income), increased spending (direct demand). Used to fight recessions.

**A** describes contractionary fiscal policy.
**C** is neither.

questions.stem: Automatic fiscal stabilisers *most likely* include:

choices.text: Income taxes and unemployment benefits.
Central bank interest rate decisions.
Discretionary stimulus packages.

questions.explanation:
Automatic stabilisers: tax revenue rises with income (cushion booms); unemployment benefits rise with joblessness (support recession). Act without political process.

**B** is monetary policy, not fiscal.
**C** is discretionary fiscal action.

questions.stem: Time lags in fiscal policy *most likely* include:

choices.text: Recognition lag, decision lag, implementation lag, effect lag.
Currency lag, trade lag, capital lag, debt lag.
Inflation lag, growth lag, unemployment lag, interest lag.

questions.explanation:
Standard lags: recognition (identify need), decision (political process), implementation (operational), effect (economic impact). Total typically 6-18 months.

**B** and **C** are not the standard fiscal lag categories.

questions.stem: When real interest rate (r) on government debt exceeds real GDP growth (g), debt-to-GDP *most likely*:

choices.text: Falls even with a primary deficit.
Rises even with a balanced primary budget.
Remains constant regardless of primary balance.

questions.explanation:
Debt dynamics: $\Delta(D/GDP) = \text{Primary Deficit} + (r-g) \cdot (D/GDP)$.

When $r > g$: even with primary balance (= 0), debt-to-GDP rises due to compounding. Vicious cycle.

**A** would be the case when $r < g$.
**C** ignores debt dynamics.

questions.stem: The Keynesian fiscal multiplier *most likely*:

choices.text: Is typically less than 1 due to crowding-out.
Is typically greater than 1 in recessions (with slack), suggesting fiscal stimulus is amplified.
Is always exactly 1 regardless of conditions.

questions.explanation:
Keynesian view: fiscal multipliers exceed 1 in recessions (slack, low rates, idle resources). Each pound of spending generates multiple pounds of GDP growth.

Empirically: ~1.5 in deep recessions; closer to 1.0 in normal times; less in overheated conditions.

**A** is classical view (less generally accepted in deep recessions).
**C** is incorrect — depends on conditions.

questions.stem: When monetary and fiscal policies conflict (e.g., monetary tightening + fiscal expansion), *most likely*:

choices.text: Monetary policy must do more to achieve its inflation target.
Both cancel out, leaving no net effect.
Fiscal policy always dominates.

questions.explanation:
When monetary pulls one direction (tightening for inflation) and fiscal pulls the other (expansion for growth), monetary must work harder. Recent example: 2022-2024 US — Fed raised rates aggressively while fiscal remained expansionary.

**B** is incorrect — there's a net effect.
**C** is incorrect — both matter.

questions.stem: Geopolitical risk for investors *most likely* includes:

choices.text: Sanctions, trade restrictions, conflicts, and supply chain disruptions.
Only military conflicts.
Only currency exchange rate movements.

questions.explanation:
Geopolitical risk is broad: economic restrictions (sanctions, tariffs), military conflicts, supply chain disruptions, political instability, regulatory shifts.

**B** is too narrow.
**C** is currency-specific risk, a subset of broader geopolitical.

questions.stem: Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine *most likely* caused for Western investors holding Russian assets:

choices.text: Minimal disruption due to natural risk diversification.
Comprehensive sanctions resulting in effectively zero value for many Russian holdings.
Increased returns due to commodity gains.

questions.explanation:
Comprehensive Western sanctions in response to invasion: SWIFT cut-off, reserves frozen, equity suspensions, delistings. Western investors' Russian holdings effectively worth zero in portfolios.

**A** misjudges concentration risk in country-specific exposures.
**C** would apply to Russian-currency-paying owners, not Western investors.

questions.stem: The trend of *globalisation reversal* since 2015 *most likely* shows:

choices.text: Continued expansion of cross-border trade.
Higher tariffs, slower trade growth, friend-shoring, and near-shoring.
Reduction in supply chain costs across all industries.

questions.explanation:
Post-2015 trends include rising tariffs (especially US-China), slowing trade growth, friend-shoring (sourcing from allies), and near-shoring (closer to home markets).

**A** is the pre-2015 trend.
**C** misjudges — globalisation reversal typically raises costs.

questions.stem: Country risk for portfolio investors *most likely* includes:

choices.text: Political stability, currency convertibility, regulatory environment, sanctions exposure.
Only sovereign debt rating.
Only currency exchange rate.

questions.explanation:
Country risk is multi-dimensional: political stability (government, elections), macroeconomic (debt, inflation), regulatory (rule of law, property rights), and external (sanctions, conflict).

**B** is too narrow.
**C** is too narrow.

questions.stem: Sanctions *most likely* affect investment portfolios by:

choices.text: Forcing divestment from named entities and reducing the value of specific holdings.
Having no effect on portfolios.
Increasing the value of all related assets.

questions.explanation:
Sanctions force divestment from named entities, freeze assets, restrict transactions. Direct effects on portfolios with exposure.

**B** and **C** misread the impact.

questions.stem: Tools of economic geopolitical influence *most likely* include:

choices.text: Tariffs, sanctions, export controls, foreign aid, currency interventions.
Only military force.
Only cultural exchanges.

questions.explanation:
Economic tools: tariffs (taxes on imports), sanctions (restrictions on transactions), export controls (technology restrictions), foreign aid (carrots/sticks), currency interventions.

**B** is military, separate category.
**C** is soft power, distinct.

questions.stem: *Comparative advantage* *most likely* differs from *absolute advantage* because:

choices.text: Comparative advantage is based on opportunity cost, not absolute productivity.
Comparative advantage requires the country to be most productive in everything.
They are the same concept.

questions.explanation:
Absolute advantage: producing with fewer inputs. Comparative advantage: lowest opportunity cost. Comparative is the key concept because it shows that even non-absolutely-advantageous countries can gain from trade.

**B** is reversed; absolute advantage requires that.
**C** is incorrect — they're distinct concepts.

questions.stem: Tariffs on imports *most likely* benefit:

choices.text: Domestic producers; harm domestic consumers.
All domestic stakeholders equally.
Foreign exporters.

questions.explanation:
Tariffs raise prices for imports → domestic producers face less competition → benefit. Consumers pay higher prices → harmed. Net effect typically negative (consumer losses exceed producer gains).

**B** treats producers and consumers identically — they're not.
**C** is opposite — foreign exporters lose sales.

questions.stem: An *import quota* differs from a *tariff* *most likely* because:

choices.text: Quotas restrict quantity; tariffs raise price. Quotas don't generate government revenue.
Quotas raise prices more than tariffs.
Quotas and tariffs are identical in all respects.

questions.explanation:
Tariff = tax per imported unit (government revenue). Quota = quantitative limit (no government revenue; rents go to those who get permits or to foreign producers if they're scarce). Both reduce imports and raise domestic prices.

**B** misreads — both have similar effects on prices.
**C** ignores the revenue-generation difference.

questions.stem: The Ricardian model of comparative advantage *most likely* emphasises:

choices.text: Technology differences between countries as the source of trade.
Resource endowments as the source of trade.
Pure market structure differences.

questions.explanation:
Ricardo's model: technology and productivity differences drive comparative advantage. Different production possibility frontiers due to technology.

**B** describes Heckscher-Ohlin model (factor endowments).
**C** is more market structure, not the comparative advantage framework.

questions.stem: Net welfare effect of tariffs in the imposing country is *most likely*:

choices.text: Net positive — protect domestic industry.
Net negative — consumer losses exceed producer + government gains.
Net zero — all effects cancel.

questions.explanation:
Economic analysis shows: domestic consumer losses (higher prices) exceed gains to domestic producers (less competition) and government (tariff revenue). Net welfare is reduced.

Exceptions: optimal tariff theory (very large countries), strategic sectors.

**A** and **C** misjudge the standard welfare analysis.

questions.stem: The WTO (World Trade Organization) is *most likely*:

choices.text: A global institution setting rules for international trade and resolving disputes.
A regional trade bloc covering Western Europe only.
An advisory body without enforcement powers.

questions.explanation:
WTO (formed 1995, successor to GATT): 164 member countries. Sets rules, resolves disputes, monitors trade barriers.

**B** confuses with EU.
**C** is incorrect — has dispute resolution and limited enforcement powers.

questions.stem: The balance of payments *most likely* consists of:

choices.text: Current account + Capital account + Financial account.
Only the current account.
GDP - National Debt.

questions.explanation:
Balance of payments has three sections: current (trade in goods/services + income), capital (cross-border transfers), financial (cross-border investment). Identity: sum = 0 (with errors/omissions).

**B** is incomplete.
**C** is unrelated.

questions.stem: A country with a *persistent current account deficit* *most likely*:

choices.text: Is receiving net capital inflows to finance the deficit.
Has no foreign investment.
Has an oversupply of currency.

questions.explanation:
Current account deficit means net imports + outflows of income exceed exports + inflows. The deficit must be financed by net capital inflows (foreign borrowing or asset sales).

US persistently runs current account deficit, financed by global appetite for USD assets.

**B** and **C** misread the relationship.

questions.stem: The FX market is *most likely*:

choices.text: A centralised exchange with daily trading limits.
The largest financial market by trading volume, with continuous 24-hour trading on weekdays.
Only available to central banks.

questions.explanation:
FX is the largest market (over $7 trillion daily), decentralised, trading ~24 hours weekdays (overlapping Tokyo, London, New York sessions).

**A** is incorrect — decentralised, not exchange-based.
**C** is incorrect — open to many participants.

questions.stem: A *fixed exchange rate regime* *most likely* requires the country to:

choices.text: Have unlimited monetary policy flexibility.
Give up independent monetary policy to maintain the peg.
Pay no attention to capital flows.

questions.explanation:
Impossible Trinity: a country can have only two of three: free capital movement, fixed exchange rate, independent monetary policy.

Fixed rate + open capital → must surrender monetary policy independence (rates set to defend peg).

Hong Kong, Saudi Arabia (USD pegs) demonstrate this trade-off.

**A** and **C** misread the constraints.

questions.stem: Higher domestic interest rates relative to other countries *most likely* cause the domestic currency to:

choices.text: Depreciate due to inflation concerns.
Appreciate due to capital inflows seeking yield.
Remain unchanged — interest rates don't affect FX.

questions.explanation:
Higher rates attract foreign capital seeking yield → currency appreciation. Demand-supply: more buyers of domestic currency for investment.

2022-2024: US rate hikes drove USD higher vs EUR, JPY, GBP.

**A** reverses the relationship.
**C** ignores the mechanism.

questions.stem: Hot money flows are *most likely*:

choices.text: Long-term foreign direct investment in factories and equipment.
Short-term, highly mobile capital flows seeking yield or speculative gains.
Reserves held by central banks.

questions.explanation:
Hot money: short-term, mobile capital. Sensitive to interest rates and risk sentiment. Can leave quickly during stress, contributing to crises.

**A** describes FDI (much more stable).
**C** is reserve flows.

questions.stem: Given USD/JPY = 150 and EUR/USD = 1.08, the EUR/JPY cross-rate is *closest* to:
questions.explanation:
Cross-rate: EUR/JPY = EUR/USD × USD/JPY = 1.08 × 150 = 162.

Meaning: 1 EUR = 162 JPY.

**A** has incorrect calculation.
**C** is the inverse (JPY/EUR).

questions.stem: Interest rate parity *most likely* implies that the currency with the *higher* interest rate will:

choices.text: Trade at a forward premium.
Trade at a forward discount.
Trade at the same forward rate as spot.

questions.explanation:
IRP: $F = S \cdot (1 + r_q) / (1 + r_b)$. Currency with higher rate is the base; forward rate is *lower* in terms of quote currency (i.e., the high-rate currency trades at forward discount).

No arbitrage condition.

**A** is reversed.
**C** would only be the case for equal interest rates.

questions.stem: Spot EUR/USD = 1.10. 1-year USD rate = 5%; 1-year EUR rate = 3%. Forward 1-year EUR/USD via IRP is *closest* to:
questions.explanation:
$F = S \cdot (1 + r_{USD}) / (1 + r_{EUR}) = 1.10 \cdot 1.05 / 1.03 = 1.10 \cdot 1.0194 = 1.121$.

EUR has lower rate → forward premium → forward EUR/USD higher than spot.

**A** uses incorrect ratio direction.
**C** is spot only.

questions.stem: Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) *most likely* says that:

choices.text: Exchange rates immediately adjust to equate purchasing power across countries.
In the long run, exchange rate changes approximate the inflation differential between countries.
Exchange rates are unrelated to inflation.

questions.explanation:
Relative PPP: $\%\Delta S \approx \pi_{foreign} - \pi_{domestic}$. Long-term concept; weakly held in short term (other factors dominate).

**A** is too strong — PPP holds in the long run only.
**C** is incorrect — PPP is the inflation-FX relationship.

questions.stem: A currency at a *forward premium* relative to spot *most likely* has:

choices.text: Higher interest rate than the counter currency.
Lower interest rate than the counter currency.
Same interest rate as the counter currency.

questions.explanation:
Lower interest rate currency trades at forward premium (compensates for lower interest earnings).

Example: EUR with 3% vs USD with 5% — EUR has forward premium in USD terms.

**A** is reversed.
**C** would mean no forward premium.

questions.stem: Triangular arbitrage opportunities *most likely* exist when:

choices.text: The direct exchange rate between two currencies differs from the cross-rate calculated via a third currency.
The three currencies have identical interest rates.
Markets are extremely liquid.

questions.explanation:
If EUR/JPY direct quote differs from EUR/USD × USD/JPY cross-rate, arbitrage profits exist. Liquid markets keep this small or zero in practice.

**B** is unrelated.
**C** is when arbitrage opportunities are minimal — the opposite of when they exist.

questions.stem: Which of the following is *most likely* a tool of monetary policy used by modern central banks?

choices.text: Setting income tax rates.
Adjusting government spending on infrastructure.
Conducting open market operations in government securities.

questions.explanation:
Open market operations — buying or selling government bonds — directly change banking-system reserves and short-term rates. This is a core monetary policy tool.

**A** and **B** are fiscal policy levers, controlled by government / legislature, not the central bank.

questions.stem: A central bank lowers its policy rate from 4% to 3%. The *most likely* short-run consequences are:

choices.text: domestic currency strengthens, bond prices fall, equity markets fall.
domestic currency weakens, bond prices rise, equity markets typically rise.
no effect on currency, bond prices, or equity markets — those depend only on long-run expectations.

questions.explanation:
Lower domestic rates → currency less attractive to hold → weakens. Bond prices rise (lower yields). Equity markets typically rally (lower discount rate, supportive of valuations and borrowing).

**A** has all directions reversed.

**C** is wrong — short-run effects are real and significant; long-run effects are an additional layer.

questions.stem: Which of the following is *most likely* a limitation of monetary policy?

choices.text: Its effects on inflation are nearly instantaneous, giving little time for adjustment.
It is poorly suited to addressing inflation caused by supply-side shocks.
It can be implemented without any concern for fiscal policy positioning.

questions.explanation:
**Supply shocks** (oil price spikes, supply-chain disruptions) cause cost-push inflation that monetary tightening can't easily address — raising rates won't fix the supply. Worse, tightening into a supply shock risks recession.

**A** is the opposite of correct — monetary policy has substantial lags (12-24 months).

**C** ignores that monetary and fiscal policy interact significantly.

questions.stem: When a central bank is at the *zero lower bound* on conventional rates, it *most likely* extends its policy through:

choices.text: raising reserve requirements aggressively.
quantitative easing — large-scale asset purchases — and forward guidance.
imposing capital controls to limit currency outflows.

questions.explanation:
At the ZLB, conventional rate cuts run out. Unconventional tools include **QE** (expand balance sheet via asset purchases) and **forward guidance** (commit to keeping rates low).

**A** would tighten policy — opposite of what's needed.

**C** is a desperate emerging-market move, not standard developed-market practice.

questions.stem: Which characteristic *most contributes* to an effective central bank?

choices.text: Direct control by the executive branch of government.
Frequent changes in stated targets to respond to political conditions.
Independence from short-term political pressure, combined with transparent communication.

questions.explanation:
**Independence + transparency** anchor long-run inflation expectations. The track record of credible delivery is what makes monetary policy actually work.

**A** historically links to higher persistent inflation (governments prefer easy policy).

**B** destroys credibility — once expectations de-anchor, they're hard to restore.

questions.stem: If a central bank reduces its policy rate while inflation expectations remain anchored at the 2% target, the *real* interest rate has *most likely*:

choices.text: risen, regardless of the size of the rate cut.
fallen, making monetary policy more expansionary.
remained unchanged — only nominal rates moved.

questions.explanation:
Real rate $\approx$ nominal − inflation expectation. If nominal falls and expectations are unchanged, real rate falls → more expansionary stance.

**A** has the direction backwards.

**C** confuses nominal and real — they move together only when inflation expectations move with them, which they don't here.

questions.stem: **Perfect competition** *most accurately* features:

choices.text: A single seller with pricing power
Many small firms producing identical products with no pricing power
A few firms with strong differentiation

questions.explanation:
Perfect competition: many firms, identical products, no barriers to entry, no pricing power (price-takers). Long-run economic profit = 0.

Real-world approximations: agricultural commodities, foreign exchange spot.

**A** describes monopoly.

**C** describes oligopoly.

questions.stem: An **oligopoly** firm *most likely* makes pricing decisions:

choices.text: Independently with no regard for competitors
Strategically, anticipating competitor responses (often modelled by game theory)
By regulator-mandated pricing schedule

questions.explanation:
Oligopoly: few large firms, interdependent decisions. Each must anticipate rivals' responses.

Tools: Cournot, Bertrand, kinked demand, prisoner's dilemma.

Examples: telecoms, airlines, cement, autos.

**A** is monopolistic competition / perfect competition.

**C** is regulated industry, not generic oligopoly.

questions.stem: The **Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI)** *most accurately* measures:

choices.text: Industry inflation rate
Market concentration, calculated as sum of squared market shares
Average industry profitability

questions.explanation:
HHI = Σ(market share %)². Range: 0 (perfectly competitive) to 10,000 (monopoly).

US antitrust thresholds:
- < 1,500: unconcentrated
- 1,500-2,500: moderate
- > 2,500: highly concentrated

Used by DOJ/FTC in merger reviews.

**A** and **C** are unrelated.

questions.stem: **Leading indicators** are *most accurately* economic data that:

choices.text: Lag the business cycle
Move ahead of the business cycle, providing forecast signals
Coincide exactly with GDP

questions.explanation:
Leading indicators: PMI, housing starts, stock prices, yield curve. Used by economists to forecast 6-12 months ahead.

Lagging: unemployment, inflation (peak after recession).
Coincident: GDP, industrial production, employment.

**A** describes lagging.

**C** describes coincident.

questions.stem: An **inverted yield curve** historically *most accurately*:

choices.text: Predicts strong economic growth
Has preceded most US recessions in the past 50 years
Has no signalling value

questions.explanation:
Inverted yield curve (short rates > long rates): typically signals expected rate cuts → weak growth. Preceded 7 of last 8 US recessions, often by 6-18 months.

Not deterministic — can be delayed or fail. Strong empirical indicator.

**A** has direction wrong.

**C** ignores historical record.

questions.stem: **Stagflation** is *most accurately*:

choices.text: High inflation with high growth
High inflation combined with stagnant growth and high unemployment
Deflation with low unemployment

questions.explanation:
Stagflation: simultaneously high inflation + economic stagnation. Defies standard Phillips curve logic.

Classic example: 1970s US/UK after oil shocks.

Difficult for policymakers — tightening worsens stagnation; loosening worsens inflation.

**A** and **C** misdescribe.

questions.stem: **Expansionary fiscal policy** *most accurately* involves:

choices.text: Raising taxes and reducing government spending
Cutting taxes and/or increasing government spending to boost demand
Central bank rate cuts

questions.explanation:
Expansionary fiscal: increase G or decrease T → boosts aggregate demand. Used in recessions.

Contrasted with monetary policy (central bank rate moves).

**A** is contractionary.

**C** is monetary policy, not fiscal.

questions.stem: **Crowding out** *most accurately* refers to:

choices.text: Government spending displacing private investment by raising interest rates
Foreigners buying up local assets
Tax cuts increasing private consumption

questions.explanation:
Crowding out: government deficit spending → bond issuance → higher interest rates → reduced private investment and consumption.

Reduces effectiveness of fiscal expansion. Magnitude debated empirically.

**B** is portfolio inflows.

**C** is the intended fiscal mechanism, not crowding out.

questions.stem: The **fiscal multiplier** is *most accurately*:

choices.text: Always exactly 1
The change in GDP per dollar of fiscal stimulus, typically estimated at 0.5-2 depending on conditions
Equal to the tax rate

questions.explanation:
Fiscal multiplier: $\Delta GDP / \Delta G$ (or $\Delta T$).

Larger when:
- Economy below potential (slack)
- Monetary policy accommodative
- Closed economy
- Stimulus reaches high-MPC recipients

Smaller when crowding out strong or open economy with leaks to imports.

Typical IMF estimates: 0.5-1.5 in normal times; higher (1-2.5) during zero-bound monetary policy.

**A** and **C** are oversimplifications.

questions.stem: **Open market operations** *most accurately* involve:

choices.text: Central bank buying/selling government bonds to influence the money supply
Treasury issuing new debt
FX intervention

questions.explanation:
OMO: primary monetary policy tool. Central bank buys bonds → money supply expands, rates fall. Sells bonds → money supply shrinks, rates rise.

Fed conducts daily OMO via primary dealers.

**B** is Treasury operations, separate from monetary policy.

**C** is FX intervention, distinct (though related).

questions.stem: **Quantitative easing (QE)** *most accurately*:

choices.text: Lowers short-term policy rates
Central bank purchases of longer-dated assets to lower long-term rates and stimulate when short rates are at zero
Tightens monetary policy

questions.explanation:
QE: unconventional monetary policy. When short rates ≈ 0 (zero bound), central bank buys long-dated bonds and MBS → lowers long rates → boosts asset prices, lending, growth.

Used extensively post-2008 and during COVID.

QT (quantitative tightening) = reverse.

**A** describes standard rate-setting.

**C** has direction reversed.

questions.stem: **Central bank independence** is *most accurately* valued because:

choices.text: It allows central banks to ignore inflation
Insulates monetary policy from short-term political pressures, improving inflation credibility
It gives central banks taxation authority

questions.explanation:
Independent central banks resist political pressure to inflate before elections, monetise debt, etc. Empirical evidence: more independent CBs achieve lower long-term inflation.

Examples: Fed (semi-independent), ECB (very independent), BOJ (formalised 1998).

Counter-examples: some EM CBs lack effective independence → higher inflation.

**A** is opposite.

**C** is wrong category.

questions.stem: **Geopolitical risk** *most accurately* refers to:

choices.text: Risk of natural disasters
Risk from international conflict, sanctions, regime change, or government action affecting investments
Currency volatility only

questions.explanation:
Geopolitical risk: conflict (wars, sanctions), policy uncertainty, regime changes, expropriation, regulatory regime shifts.

Major examples: Russia 2022 (sanctions), China-US trade tensions, Middle East conflicts, Brexit.

Affects equity risk premium, sovereign yields, FX, commodity prices.

**A** is natural disaster risk.

**C** is too narrow.

questions.stem: **Sanctions** on a country *most likely* affect investors via:

choices.text: Frozen assets, restricted transactions, compliance burden, market access loss
Higher dividends from sanctioned companies
No effect on financial markets

questions.explanation:
Sanctions: asset freezes, transaction bans, blocked payments, secondary sanctions on third parties. Investors holding sanctioned assets may face stranded positions.

Russia 2022: hundreds of billions in Russian assets frozen; foreign investors unable to repatriate.

**B** is wrong.

**C** is contradicted by extensive evidence.

questions.stem: **'De-globalisation' or fragmentation** in global trade is *most likely* to:

choices.text: Increase global growth via specialisation
Raise inflation, reduce supply chain efficiency, and lower global growth potential
Have no effect on inflation

questions.explanation:
Globalisation 1980-2010s: drove low inflation, efficient supply chains, lower global poverty.

Fragmentation (US-China decoupling, friendshoring, sanctions): higher trade costs, redundant supply chains, less specialisation, higher inflation.

IMF estimates: fragmentation could reduce global GDP 0.2-7% over time.

**A** describes globalisation.

**C** ignores supply chain effects on prices.

questions.stem: **Comparative advantage** (Ricardo) *most accurately* says countries should:

choices.text: Produce only what they need domestically
Specialise in goods where they have the lowest opportunity cost, then trade
Trade only with neighbouring countries

questions.explanation:
Comparative advantage: even if Country A is better at everything (absolute advantage), both countries gain by A specialising in its biggest advantage and B in its smallest disadvantage. Opportunity cost determines specialisation.

Cornerstone of international trade theory.

**A** is autarky.

**C** is geographic, not economic logic.

questions.stem: **Tariffs** on imports *most likely*:

choices.text: Reduce domestic prices for consumers
Raise prices for consumers, protect some domestic producers, but reduce overall economic efficiency
Always boost overall employment

questions.explanation:
Tariff: import tax. Effects:
- Higher prices for consumers
- Protected domestic producers (winners)
- Imported goods more expensive → less consumed
- Net deadweight loss to economy
- Foreign trading partners may retaliate

Evidence from US-China tariffs 2018-2019: prices rose, manufacturing employment barely changed.

**A** and **C** are common myths.

questions.stem: **Balance of payments** = current account + capital account. A persistent **current account deficit** *most likely* implies:

choices.text: Surplus on capital account (foreign capital inflows)
Surplus on current account also
Government surplus

questions.explanation:
BoP must balance. Current account deficit (imports > exports) requires capital account surplus (foreign capital inflows finance the deficit).

US example: persistent CA deficit financed by foreign Treasury buying.

Reversal of capital flows can trigger BoP crisis (sudden stop).

**B** contradicts BoP identity.

**C** is unrelated (government budget is separate).

questions.stem: **Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)** *most accurately*:

choices.text: Short-term portfolio investment in foreign stocks
Long-term cross-border investment with management control (typically ≥10% ownership)
Currency trading

questions.explanation:
FDI: long-term cross-border investment with significant control. Typical 10%+ ownership threshold.

Examples: building a factory abroad, acquiring foreign subsidiary, joint ventures.

Distinct from portfolio investment (passive, can flow quickly).

**A** is portfolio investment.

**C** is FX trading.

questions.stem: **'Sudden stop' capital outflows** *most accurately* are:

choices.text: Gradual reduction of capital inflows
Rapid reversal of foreign capital, often triggering currency crisis and recession
Planned monetary policy

questions.explanation:
Sudden stop: foreign investors rapidly withdraw capital. Causes:
- Sharp currency depreciation
- Inability to service foreign-denominated debt
- Banking crisis (foreign funding lost)
- Economic recession

Classic examples: Asian crisis 1997, Argentina 2001, Turkey 2018.

**A** is gradual.

**C** is not policy.

questions.stem: **Capital controls** in emerging markets are *most likely* used to:

choices.text: Promote global capital allocation
Limit short-term portfolio flows to reduce currency volatility and financial instability risk
Increase taxes

questions.explanation:
Capital controls: restrictions on cross-border capital flows. Targets:
- Short-term portfolio flows (hot money)
- Outflows during crisis (Iceland 2008, Greece 2015)
- Inflows during boom (Brazil 2009-2011)

IMF historically opposed but now acknowledges role for selective use.

Trade-off: stability vs market efficiency, FDI deterrent.

**A** is opposite.

**C** is unrelated.

questions.stem: **Purchasing Power Parity (PPP)** *most accurately* predicts that:

choices.text: Exchange rates have no relationship to prices
Exchange rates adjust to equalise the purchasing power of currencies across countries
Inflation has no effect on FX

questions.explanation:
PPP: same basket of goods should cost the same in any currency after FX conversion.

Absolute PPP: prices equalise (rarely holds short-term).
Relative PPP: FX moves equal inflation differential (holds better long-term).

Big Mac index = informal absolute PPP gauge.

**A** and **C** contradict the theory.

questions.stem: Under **interest rate parity (IRP)**, if USD rates exceed JPY rates, the **forward USDJPY** *most likely*:

choices.text: Trades below spot (USD at forward discount; equivalently JPY at forward premium)
Trades above spot (USD at forward premium)
Equals spot exactly

questions.explanation:
IRP: $F = S \cdot (1+r_{quote})/(1+r_{base})$. 

Quote convention USDJPY: USD = base, JPY = quote. If $r_{USD} > r_{JPY}$, the higher-yield currency (USD) trades at forward **discount** — i.e., forward USDJPY < spot. Equivalently, JPY trades at forward **premium**.

This no-arbitrage relation prevents free lunch from borrowing in low-yield and investing in high-yield without offsetting via the forward.

**B** has direction reversed.

**C** ignores rate differential.

questions.stem: A **carry trade** strategy *most likely* involves:

choices.text: Borrowing in low-yield currency and investing in high-yield currency, profiting from rate differential
Borrowing and lending in same currency
Hedging all currency exposure

questions.explanation:
Carry trade: borrow in low-yield (e.g., JPY, CHF) and invest in high-yield (e.g., AUD, EM). Profit = interest differential, assuming FX doesn't move adversely.

IRP says expected return is zero in equilibrium, but empirically carry trades earn positive return (forward premium puzzle) — at cost of crash risk.

**B** is funding mismatch, not carry.

**C** eliminates the carry.
